documents.unit: ACU Library (Faculty Guide: AI and ChatGPT)
documents.title: Faculty Guide: AI and ChatGPT: Academic Integrity
documents.summary: A library faculty guide that tells instructors to define acceptable AI use in their own syllabus, lists what a syllabus statement should contain, and gives MLA and APA citation formats for AI. It offers three example statements (AI required, AI prohibited, AI only with permission) borrowed from Harvard and Colorado State. It sets no university-wide rule.
documents.stance_why: The guide says 'Best practice is to define what is acceptable and not acceptable in your class' and supplies three template statements (required, prohibited, use-with-permission) for instructors to choose from, so it decides nothing itself and hands the decision to instructors, with tiers listed.

units.why: The guide gives MLA's format for citing generative AI output ('Name of AI tool, version of AI tool, Company, Date of chat, URL'); it names tool, version and date, so P25 rather than the generic P24. Addressed to students, who do the citing, as guidance (should).
units.anchor: Name of AI tool, version of AI tool, Company, Date of chat, URL.
units.frag_start: Description of chat
units.policy: Students cite AI chats in MLA with the description of the chat as the prompt, then the name and version of the AI tool, the company, the date of the chat and the URL.
units.resolution_why: Both coders chose P25, student, should. They differed on unit_stance (A require, B neutral) and on whether the anchor alone states the rule. The anchor lists citation elements but does not say they are a citation format, so I kept A's normalized policy, which matches the source. A citation duty is a disclosure duty, so unit_stance is require.

units.why: 'If you create a shareable link to the chat transcript, include that instead of the tool's URL' tells students what to put in the citation, so it is a citation-detail rule (P25).
units.anchor: If you create a shareable link to the chat transcript, include that instead
units.frag_start: If you create a shareable
units.policy: If students create a shareable link to the chat transcript, they include it instead of the tool's URL in the MLA citation.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B found this. The source has the sentence 'If you create a shareable link to the chat transcript, include that instead of the tool's URL', a real citation rule, so I kept it. I wrote a policy because the anchor omits that it applies to the MLA citation.

units.why: 'MLA also recommends acknowledging when you used the tool in a note or your text' recommends acknowledging AI use in the submission, so it is disclosure (P24), should because it is a recommendation.
units.anchor: MLA also recommends acknowledging when you used the tool in a note or your text
units.frag_start: MLA also recommends acknowledging when
units.resolution_why: Both coders chose P24, student, should. They differed on unit_stance (A require, B permit). The source recommends that students acknowledge AI use, a disclosure duty rather than a permission, so require. The anchor states the rule, so policy is null.

units.why: The same sentence recommends 'verifying any sources or citations the tool supplies', which tells students to check AI output, so P31, should.
units.anchor: verifying any sources or citations the tool supplies
units.frag_start: MLA also recommends acknowledging when
units.resolution_why: Both coders chose P31, student, should, neutral. Only the topic labels differed; I kept A's accountability-understanding plus disclosure-citation because the sentence is about checking sources and citations.

units.why: 'It may be worthwhile to include the chat's transcript as an appendix to your project' is an optional recommendation to keep and submit the transcript, so P26 with may.
units.anchor: It may be worthwhile to include the chat's transcript as an appendix to your project.
units.frag_start: It may be worthwhile to include
units.resolution_why: Both coders chose P26, student, may. They differed on unit_stance (A permit, B neutral). The source makes the transcript optional ('may be worthwhile'), which fits permit.

units.why: 'Use the company as the author, not the tool's name' and 'Include a brief description of the chat indicating the prompts in square brackets' are detailed APA citation requirements naming company and prompts, so P25.
units.anchor: Include a brief description of the chat indicating the prompts in square brackets.
units.frag_start: Use the company as the author,
units.resolution_why: Only coder B found this. The source contains these APA citation instructions, a real rule of the same kind as the other P25 units, so I kept it. Unit_stance is require to match the other citation units; the anchor states the prompt-description rule, so policy is null.

units.why: For chats that cannot be shared or retrieved, the guide says to 'follow APA guidelines for citing personal communication' with 'only an in-text citation'; it is a specific citation-format rule, so P25, should.
units.anchor: only include an in-text citation and do not include an entry in the references list
units.frag_start: If you have not saved the chat
units.policy: When a chat transcript is not saved or cannot be shared or retrieved, students cite it as personal communication with an in-text citation only and no entry in the references list.
units.resolution_why: Both coders chose P25, student, should. They differed on unit_stance (A require, B neutral) and on writing a policy. The anchor omits the personal-communication condition, so I kept A's policy, which follows the source. Citation duty, so require.

units.why: 'Conversations with students reveal that they are uncertain about what levels of AI use are appropriate' and campus definitions 'may not be clear' is the stated reason for defining expectations in each class; it informs the expectation-setting type P09 and sets no rule itself.
units.anchor: our campus definitions of plagiarism and cheating may not be clear
units.frag_start: Conversations with students reveal that
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded P04, instructor, before-course. Coder B coded UNCOVERED, all, general. The passage says students are unsure about acceptable AI use and campus definitions are unclear; the next sentence, 'Best practice is to define what is acceptable and not acceptable in your class', is the response. It says nothing about who decides, so P04 does not fit. It is the rationale for stating expectations (P09), so UNCOVERED is not needed. Actor is instructor because the faculty guide addresses faculty; phase is general because it is a rationale (B).

units.why: 'Best practice is to define what is acceptable and not acceptable in your class. Be transparent upfront.' tells instructors to state their AI expectations, so P09 with should because it is called best practice.

units.why: The syllabus statement 'should include' circumstances when AI use is 'permitted or forbidden'; this tells instructors to state the AI rule in the syllabus (P09) and leaves the rule itself to them.
units.anchor: Under what circumstances AI use is permitted or forbidden

units.policy: A syllabus AI policy should state under what circumstances AI use is permitted or forbidden.
units.resolution_why: Both coders chose P09, instructor, should. They differed on phase (A course-start, B before-course). The rule is what the syllabus statement tells students, which the codebook places in course-start (communicating expectations), so course-start. I applied the same phase to the other four bullets of this list.

units.why: The bullet 'How students should cite or credit AI' asks instructors to put citation expectations in the syllabus. Its content is crediting AI, so P24; the actor is the instructor who writes the statement.

units.why: 'the need to use AI as a tool to learn, not just to produce content' says AI should support students' learning rather than replace it, which matches P32 rather than P41 because it is directive and framed as a syllabus content item.

units.why: Example 1 says 'I expect you to use AI (e.g., ChatGPT and image generation tools) in this class', so AI use is expected by default: P02. 'Expect' is an expectation rather than a hard requirement, so should; unit stance encourage.
units.anchor: I expect you to use AI (e.g., ChatGPT and image generation tools) in this class.
units.frag_start: I expect you to use AI
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded one P02 unit (must, require, course-start) covering both sentences. Coder B coded two units: this sentence (should, encourage, during-work) and 'some assignments will require it' (must, require). The two sentences state different rules (AI is expected; some assignments require it), so I split them as B did. 'I expect' is an expectation, not a hard requirement, so should and encourage. The rule governs how students work, so during-work.

units.why: 'some assignments will require it' makes AI use mandatory on some assignments; P02 covers expected use and this is the stronger, required form.

units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this as a separate unit; coder A folded it into the previous one. The source states it as its own rule ('In fact, some assignments will require it'), so I kept it as a separate unit.

units.why: 'Learning to use AI is an emerging skill and I provide tutorials on how to use them' presents AI use as a skill the course teaches, so P44; it informs rather than binds. The speaker is the instructor ('I provide tutorials').

units.resolution_why: Coder A anchored 'If you provide minimum-effort prompts, you will get low-quality results' (informs, neutral); coder B anchored 'You will need to refine your prompts' (should, encourage). Both are P44, student, during-work and the same passage. I used B's anchor because it states the advice directly; should because it tells students what to do, encourage because it teaches effective use.

units.resolution_why: Coder A coded P01 on the sentence 'Any work written, developed, created, or inspired by AI is considered plagiarism and will not be tolerated'; coder B coded that sentence as P36 and coded 'this kind of technology does not belong' as P01. The default ban is stated most directly by 'does not belong', so I used B's P01 unit. The plagiarism sentence is coded separately below as P36 (it classifies the ban as misconduct), so both rules are kept without merging them.

units.why: 'Any work written, developed, created, or inspired by artificial intelligence (AI) is considered plagiarism and will not be tolerated' classifies AI-involved work as plagiarism; it is about how the violation is labelled, so P36 rather than P01.

units.policy: Any work written, developed, created, or inspired by AI is considered plagiarism and will not be tolerated.
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded P01 (during-work); coder B coded P36 (when-misuse). Both read the same sentence. It does two things: it bans AI-inspired work ('will not be tolerated') and labels it plagiarism. The ban is captured by the P01 unit above, so this unit takes the classification, P36. I kept must-not and when-misuse (B) because 'will not be tolerated' is a prohibition addressed to students and is enforced as misconduct.

notes: Single library guide, not an official provost policy. Examples 1-3 are quoted third-party sample statements (Harvard Mollick; Colorado State); units from them are coded as the guide's offered templates, not as ACU rules. Reconciled: 30 matched units, 6 coder-B-only units kept, 0 coder-A-only units.
